blocks.content: Right now, this very page travelled from a computer somewhere in the world to the device in your hands. It crossed cables, buildings, maybe an ocean, and arrived in a fraction of a second. The machinery that made that possible is a computer network.

This first topic answers the most fundamental question of the whole course: what actually is a network? Once this picture is clear, every later idea, IP addresses, TCP, DNS, routing, will have a place to sit.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436866314-704463389.png
1. Start With Two Computers and a Wire
blocks.text: 1. Start With Two Computers and a Wire

blocks.content: Strip everything away and a network begins with the simplest possible setup: two computers joined by one cable. If one can send data down the cable and the other can receive it, you already have a network.
Everything else in networking, and in this entire course, is just this idea scaled up: more computers, more wires, and clever machines in the middle deciding where each piece of data should go.
["Two connected computers are already a network","One sends bits, the other receives them","Everything bigger is this same idea, scaled up","The complexity lives in the middle, not at the ends"]
items: Two connected computers are already a network
One sends bits, the other receives them
Everything bigger is this same idea, scaled up
The complexity lives in the middle, not at the ends

blocks.title: The postal system in miniature
blocks.content: Two neighbours passing letters over a fence is a postal system, just a tiny one. Add streets, postmen, and sorting offices and it becomes the real thing. Networks grow exactly the same way from two computers and a wire.
2. What Exactly Is a Computer Network?
blocks.text: 2. What Exactly Is a Computer Network?

blocks.content: A computer network is a set of devices, called nodes, connected by links so they can exchange data. The nodes are computers, phones, servers, and the special machines between them; the links are the cables, fibre, and radio waves that join them.

The definition has two halves and both matter. The devices must be connected, and they must be able to exchange data. A bundle of computers in one room with no links is not a network, and neither are two machines wired together that speak completely different languages.

["Nodes: the devices, from laptops and phones to servers and routers","Links: the connections, wired like Ethernet and fibre, or wireless like WiFi","The goal: moving data between nodes reliably","Connected but unable to communicate does not count"]
items: Nodes: the devices, from laptops and phones to servers and routers
Links: the connections, wired like Ethernet and fibre, or wireless like WiFi
The goal: moving data between nodes reliably
Connected but unable to communicate does not count

blocks.content: 3. Why We Connect Computers At All
blocks.text: 3. Why We Connect Computers At All

blocks.content: Networks exist because sharing beats copying. Before networks, moving a file meant physically carrying a disk between machines, and every office needed its own printer beside every desk.
Connecting computers lets them share three things: data, resources, and communication. Every application you use daily is one of these three in disguise.

["Sharing data: websites, file transfers, streaming, this very page","Sharing resources: one printer, one storage server, one internet connection for a whole office","Communication: email, chat, video calls, multiplayer games","Scale: one server can serve millions because the network carries its answers everywhere"]
items: Sharing data: websites, file transfers, streaming, this very page
Sharing resources: one printer, one storage server, one internet connection for a whole office
Communication: email, chat, video calls, multiplayer games
Scale: one server can serve millions because the network carries its answers everywhere

blocks.title: Why this matters for engineers
blocks.content: Every system you will ever design, every API call, database query, and microservice, is computers talking over a network. Understanding the wire under your software is what separates guessing from engineering.
4. The Building Blocks
Real networks are built from a small cast of characters, and you will meet them again and again through this course. Each has one clear job.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436866316-428280851.png

["Hosts: the devices at the edge that actually use the network, your laptop, your phone, a server","Switch: connects devices within one local network, like all the machines in an office","Router: connects different networks together and chooses paths between them","Links: the wires, fibre, and radio connecting everything"]
items: Hosts: the devices at the edge that actually use the network, your laptop, your phone, a server
Switch: connects devices within one local network, like all the machines in an office
Router: connects different networks together and chooses paths between them
Links: the wires, fibre, and radio connecting everything

blocks.content: A helpful way to remember the split: hosts are where data starts and ends, switches move it around inside a building, and routers move it between buildings, cities, and continents.

blocks.title: Switch vs router in one line
blocks.content: A switch says: which device inside my network should get this? A router says: which network should this go to next? Inside versus between, that is the whole difference.
5. Networks Come in Sizes
Networks are named by how much ground they cover. The acronyms sound heavy but the idea is simple: from your desk to the whole planet, each size has a name.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436866316-654348552.png

{"headers":["Type","Full name","Covers","Example"],"rows":[["PAN","Personal Area Network","A few metres","Your phone and earbuds over Bluetooth"],["LAN","Local Area Network","A building","Your home WiFi, an office network"],["MAN","Metropolitan Area Network","A city","A city wide cable network"],["WAN","Wide Area Network","Countries, continents","The links joining offices across cities"]]}

The one you interact with most directly is the LAN: your home WiFi is a LAN, and the office network is a LAN. WANs are what tie all those LANs together across long distances, and the biggest WAN of all is the internet itself.
6. The Internet: A Network of Networks
blocks.text: 6. The Internet: A Network of Networks

blocks.content: The internet is not one giant network owned by anyone. It is millions of separate networks, homes, offices, universities, data centres, that agreed to connect to each other and pass data along.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436866316-250473087.png
blocks.alt: The Internet: A Network of Networks

blocks.content: Your home LAN connects to your internet provider network, which connects to other provider networks, which connect to the networks of Google, Netflix, and every other service. Data hops from network to network, router to router, until it arrives.

["The internet is many networks voluntarily joined together","Routers are the glue between networks","No single owner: cooperation through shared rules makes it work","inter network is literally where the name internet comes from"]
items: The internet is many networks voluntarily joined together
Routers are the glue between networks
No single owner: cooperation through shared rules makes it work
inter network is literally where the name internet comes from

blocks.title: The highway system
blocks.content: No single company owns all roads. Cities build local streets, countries build highways, and they all connect at junctions. You can drive across a continent because everyone builds to compatible rules. The internet is the same, with routers as the junctions.
7. How Machines Find Each Other
With millions of connected devices, a message needs an exact destination. Networks solve this the same way the postal system does: every device gets an address.

That address is the IP address, a unique number like 142.250.183.14 that identifies a device on the network. Every packet of data carries two of them: the address it came from and the address it is going to, exactly like the sender and receiver on an envelope.

["Every connected device has an IP address","Data travels in packets, each stamped with source and destination addresses","Routers read the destination address to decide where to send the packet next","Human friendly names like google.com are translated to IP addresses by DNS, coming later in this course"]
items: Every connected device has an IP address
Data travels in packets, each stamped with source and destination addresses
Routers read the destination address to decide where to send the packet next
Human friendly names like google.com are translated to IP addresses by DNS, coming later in this course

blocks.content: Addresses, and how routers use them to find paths, get their own full section later. For now, hold the envelope picture: every piece of data knows where it is from and where it is going.
8. Protocols: The Rules of the Conversation
blocks.text: 8. Protocols: The Rules of the Conversation

blocks.content: Connecting machines is not enough; they must speak the same language. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for how data is formatted, sent, acknowledged, and repaired when things go wrong.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436866317-376747314.png
blocks.alt: Protocols: The Rules of the Conversation

blocks.content: Two people can only hold a conversation if they share a language and take turns. Protocols give machines exactly that: HTTP for web pages, TCP for reliable delivery, IP for addressing. You use dozens of them every minute without noticing.

["A protocol is a rulebook both sides agree to follow","Rules cover format, order, timing, and error handling","HTTP, TCP, IP, and DNS are all protocols you use daily","Shared protocols are why a phone in India can talk to a server in America"]
items: A protocol is a rulebook both sides agree to follow
Rules cover format, order, timing, and error handling
HTTP, TCP, IP, and DNS are all protocols you use daily
Shared protocols are why a phone in India can talk to a server in America

blocks.title: Why rules beat wires
blocks.content: The genius of the internet is not the cables, it is the agreements. Any device, from any maker, in any country, can join, because the protocols are public and shared. The rules are the network.
9. What Makes a Network Good
Not all networks feel the same. Three measurements decide whether a network feels instant or infuriating, and they will follow you through the rest of this course and into system design.

["Bandwidth: how much data can flow per second, the width of the pipe","Latency: how long one piece of data takes to arrive, the length of the pipe","Reliability: how often data arrives correctly, without loss or corruption"]
items: Bandwidth: how much data can flow per second, the width of the pipe
Latency: how long one piece of data takes to arrive, the length of the pipe
Reliability: how often data arrives correctly, without loss or corruption

blocks.content: The crucial insight is that bandwidth and latency are different things. A truck full of hard drives has enormous bandwidth but terrible latency; a satellite link can have decent bandwidth yet high latency because of the distance. Fast downloads need bandwidth; snappy video calls need low latency.

blocks.title: The pipe picture
blocks.content: Think of water pipes. Bandwidth is how wide the pipe is, latency is how long the water takes to travel through it, and reliability is whether the pipe leaks. A good network scores well on all three.
10. Key Takeaways

["A network is devices, nodes, connected by links so they can exchange data","Two computers and a wire is already a network; everything else is scale","Hosts use the network, switches connect devices inside a network, routers connect networks together","Networks are sized as PAN, LAN, MAN, and WAN, and the internet is a network of networks","Every device has an IP address, and every packet carries its source and destination","Protocols are the shared rules that let any two machines understand each other","Bandwidth, latency, and reliability measure how good a network is"]
